extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature/philosophy interested in Emerson's essays
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical essay (Emerson) exploring individuality, genius, art, and society; mixes prescriptive claims about character, government, and the nature of art and reading. Not an instructional how-to but contains many evaluative statements about art, persons, and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Art, in the artist, is proportion, or a habitual respect to the whole by an eye loving beauty in details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The eye must not lose sight for a moment of the purpose." Beautiful details are necessary but "they must be means and never other." Example contrast: "Lively boys write to their ear and eye... the cool reader finds nothing but sweet jingles in it. When they grow older, they respect the argument."

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for universals / the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Value the universal, the 'magnetism' or system, rather than isolated traits or personalities; prefer the genius (the whole habit) to particular parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deifying persons from single traits: "Let us go for universals; for the magnetism, not for the needles." A personal influence is fleeting—admire the whole disposition (habit) rather than episodic acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess by total powers and habitual system
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging a person or an author, evaluate their habitual, systematic character (their 'system') rather than solitary words or acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The genius is all. The man, -- it is his system: we do not try a solitary word or act, but his habit." Do not praise occasional departures from faith as representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reading practice (read least flattering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Read in a manner least flattering to the author to better discern the work's enduring qualities; seek the author's higher model or source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "I find the most pleasure in reading a book in a manner least flattering to the author." Example: read Proclus or Plato as mechanical aids; seek the "author's author" and attend to the master's effect (e.g., Handel's Messiah) where the genius shows through imperfect performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralizing from single excellent traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer a person's overall perfection from one shining trait; geniuses and great men have foibles and are partial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson warns: "We consecrate a great deal of nonsense because it was allowed by great men. There is none without his foible." Beware the false symmetrical portrait drawn from one arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value specialization and distributed genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature distributes different talents across many persons and roles; recognize and respect specialized, local excellence rather than seeking universal genius in one individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "She loves better a wheelwright who dreams all night of wheels, and a groom who is part of his horse; for she is full of work, and these are her hands." Expect and honor varied, localized gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anomalous facts and heterodox movements as critical diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Anomalous doctrines or movements (homoeopathy, mesmerism, Swedenborgism, Fourierism, etc.) are often poor practices but valuable as criticism on contemporary science, philosophy, or preaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "They are poor pretensions enough, but good criticism on the science, philosophy, and preaching of the day." Treat such anomalies as indications to refine mainstream thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mannerism and set stylistic tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature abhors mannerism; there is a tendency to repeat a learned trick or style indefinitely, which is to be resisted in conversation and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "It is so much easier to do what one has done before than to do a new thing, that there is a perpetual tendency to a set mode." Strive for freshness over perpetual imitation of a successful trick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor fewer laws and cultivation of private character
rubrics_metrics.description: Political and social health is better served by the growth of individual character than by multiplying laws and conferring power; the influence of private character is the antidote to government overreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Hence the less government we have the better,--the fewer laws, and the less confided power. The antidote... is the influence of private character, the growth of the Individual; the appearance of the wise man... the State expires." Evaluate institutions by how they cultivate character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize cyclic revelation of qualities (rotation of prominence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature prevents any one person from embodying all qualities at once; different attributes and persons come to prominence in succession, keeping society balanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson's image: "Your turn now, my turn next," and the rotation by which "the points come in succession to the meridian." Expect intermittent visibility of attributes rather than constant, universal presence.
